description_full: Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW) operates vibrant retail-anchored destinations in many of the world's best cities and urban areas. This powerful network attracts over 900 million customer visits annually, supports the growth of major retailers, and makes a significant social and economic contribution to local communities. This network includes 65 owned shopping centres in the US and Europe that represent around 88% of the Group's 49.5 Bn euros asset portfolio  with 41 centres operating under the iconic Westfield brand. URW also has partners who operate Westfield-branded destinations in fast-growing new markets. Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield SE was incorporated in July 23rd, 1968 in France.

CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Unibail-Rodamco SE is a large-cap real estate business with a $14.5B market cap on $3.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 63% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.3B in free cash flow — roughly 38 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.61× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 11.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 29% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sect: Its 58% operating margin runs 36pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.93x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.9% of sector revenue and 2.7% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 9% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market.
Trading is thin (about $11K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 76% in the 2020 crash, 49% in the 2022 bear market and 59% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 37% below its DCF fair value of $158, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 82%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $83.74 to $279 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/E 7.9 vs 23.9 and P/FCF 11.4 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 8.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 0.7% annual cash-flow growth, 5pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.11).
It runs a 63% gross margin and converts 38% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.61x.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.8x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 11.1x net debt to EBITDA ($3.0B of cash against $25.0B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.1x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.52 in the distress zone.
The value-trap profile is elevated (63/100); see the breakdown below.
The Beneish M-score (-1.84) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.0% over 3 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
own: Insiders own 28.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 43%.
It returns 3.7% a year to shareholders (5.2% in dividends, less 0.2% of net share issuance).
people: With about 1,933 employees, each generates about $1.7M of revenue, 0.8x the Real Estate median.
That works out to $657K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.2M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
